newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Saudis, Iran want OPEC to stop oil quota violations.
newsitem.headline: Saudis, Iran want OPEC to stop oil quota violations.

text.p: Saudi Arabia joined Iran on Tuesday to demand that other OPEC countries stop violating their production quotas, which have beaten down oil prices.
But the Saudis appeared confident that rising oil consumption later this year would support the market, even under the pressure of OPEC output that is running at a 17-year high.
Meanwhile, oil prices lost more ground on news that Iraq expects to resume oil exports under a U.N. oil-for-food pact within a week to 10 days.

Crude oil for delivery in August lost 16 cents to $18.98 a barrel in late afternoon trading on the New York Mercantile Exchange after Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Rasheed predicted an early end to delays in the next round of Iraq's sales under a pact with the United Nations that relaxes Gulf War sanctions.
"We expect to start exporting oil in the next week to 10 days and we don't anticipate any problems in discussions," Rasheed told a news conference in Madrid.
U.N. officials have also said Iraq is a week to 10 days from completing an aid distribution plan to restart sales.

The ministers of OPEC kingpin Saudi Arabia and Iran -- the cartel's second-biggest producer -- speaking to reporters prior to Wednesday's start of a ministerial conference of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, said they wanted member countries to stick to their export quotas.
The betting was that the talks would produce an agreement to freeze current quotas for six months from June 30, well-placed delegates said.
Saudi Oil Minister Ali Naimi declared that "a rollover is good if everyone adheres to their quota ... We would like everyone to honour their commitments."

He softened the blow with his assessment that oil markets could support current OPEC production, assessed by the Saudis at up to 2 million barrels daily in excess of the official 25.03 million barrel ceiling.
"Demand is good. There is no reason for prices to go lower," he told reporters.
Iran's minister, Gholamreza Aqazadeh, was blunt in saying that something had to be done about discipline if prices -- down to $19 per barrel from $25 six months ago -- were to be secure.
"Any decision without stopping the violations does not pay," he said.

Delegates said privately that apart from giving a closed session tongue-lashing to the Venezuelan minister, Erwin Arrieta, and other alleged violators, it was hard to see what the rest of OPEC could do to police better quota discipline.
Petroleos de Venezuela, the Venezuelan state oil company, has said that OPEC should abandon production quotas altogether and opt for a policy of expanding its share of the world market.
Arrieta says he will not actually demand that at this week's session, but that he would like to air ideas for change.
The Saudis, meanwhile, seem to put their trust in a seasonal, winter upswing in heating oil demand.
"The market is right now healthy," said one Gulf source. "You cannot be certain but the most likely case is that prices will improve in the third quarter."
